A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OnlineSPEC work and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Content can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting, relocated explanations and additional material in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, deployment trajectories, hyperparameter analyses and training-overhead measurements in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model evaluations, autoregressive-decoding comparisons, warm-up sensitivity and alternative-update experiments.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the principal Online-LR, Opt-Hydra and Ens-EAGLE updates remain unchanged. v2 adds Ens-Hydra, applying the existing ensemble strategy to Hydra as an alternative to optimistic updating, in Tables 4 and 9. This is a limited additional instantiation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, the mathematical MMLU subset, Code-Search-Python, Spider, MBPP and Alpaca-finance. The added experiments reuse existing task coverage; larger model configurations and different warm-up counts do not introduce new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds standard autoregressive decoding to comparisons with Opt-Hydra and Ens-EAGLE-3 on GSM8K (Tables 3 and 7), extending its earlier participation in reasoning evaluations. Ens-Hydra is also added as an alternative comparator in Tables 4 and 9. The comparator sets in retained Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged.

E3.justification: The evaluation configurations expand from three to five target models through Vicuna-13B and Qwen3-32B, with Qwen3-1.7B drafting for the latter. New protocols sweep 500, 1000 and 1500 warm-up samples and approximate environmental variation using consecutive prompt-embedding distances. These substantially extend the evaluation design; retained experiments keep their documented settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds warm-up sensitivity (Table 8), ensemble-versus-optimistic updating for Hydra (Tables 4 and 9), and an empirical illustration of theoretical trends (Figure 11). Existing learning-rate, online-duration and training-overhead analyses are retained. Figure 11 has an attribution ambiguity: its caption names Ens-EAGLE while its legend names Ens-EAGLE-3.

E5.justification: Table 2's caption changes from results averaged over three runs 'with standard deviations' to simply averaged over three runs. Neither version displays standard deviations in that table, so this corrects the reporting description rather than removing uncertainty values. Three-run reporting and the uncertainty entries in the other retained tables remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Numerical results in Tables 1–2, the original hyperparameter and overhead tables, and the existing plots are retained. New Table 3 reports 1.46× and 1.84× speedups over autoregressive decoding for Ens-EAGLE-3 and Opt-Hydra on Vicuna-13B, and 1.31× for Online-LR on Qwen3-32B, with accepted length 9.98 and accuracy 95.68%. Additional tables and Figure 11 report new comparison and sensitivity results, extending the evidence under new settings.

T1.justification: Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 receive substantive corrections. The acceleration lower bound becomes (k+1)/[(alpha*k+1)*(1+(k+1)*sqrt(Reg_T/(2T)))], and the upper bound changes from k/(alpha*k+1) to (k+1)/(alpha*k+1). Corollaries 1–3 now include saturation through min{k+1,...}. Appendix D replaces the central lower-bound derivation and propagates these changes through the proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the stated empirical scope from three to five foundation models. The central claims—a unified online-learning framework, a formal regret–acceleration connection, three principal instantiations and up to 24% speedup—remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix E qualifies the experiments as adaptation from drafts trained from scratch, rather than released checkpoints, and emphasizes framework contributions over benchmark-specific gains. v2 also interprets the new scaling and warm-up findings, revises the theoretical discussion to describe saturation, and corrects Appendix C.1's explanation from small to high acceptance rate for an accurate draft.

D1.justification: New disclosures include draft architecture and parameter counts for Hydra, EAGLE and EAGLE-3 (B.7), TPS aggregation as the mean of per-question throughput (B.10), and from-scratch initialization (E). These document existing implementation choices without establishing changed procedures. Most optimizer settings, hardware, prompts and code-access information were already present.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds brief coverage of diffusion-language-model acceleration and citations on distribution-shift adaptation and distillation; the introduction also cites Wang et al. (2026). The MATH citation changes to Hendrycks et al. (2021b), and the SRT citation is removed. The central positioning against task-specific online adaptation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording improvements, adds an organization paragraph, expands acknowledgements and introduces impact and limitation sections. The dynamic-regret rationale and theorem remarks move from appendices into Section 2.2, while some existing implementation information moves into Section 4.1. Most prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The single-column workshop format is replaced by a two-column main text and references, with extensively reflowed and resized tables, figures, equations and headers. v2 adds Tables 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 and Figure 11; Tables 4 and 9 display the same analysis. Figures 1–10 are retained and repositioned rather than scientifically redrawn.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a serious inconsistency in the central theoretical contribution: v1's acceleration lower bound could exceed its finite upper bound, whereas the revised bounds and proofs explicitly account for saturation and the additional output token. Larger-model evaluations, direct autoregressive comparisons, new sensitivity analyses and clearer initialization limitations strengthen empirical support and transparency. These gains outweigh residual reporting issues such as Figure 11's mismatched method labels.
